name: Apple

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have rich, vibrant color with no bruises or soft brown spots. Slight variations in color are normal.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm with no soft or mushy areas. A ripe apple won't give when you press it.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Pick it up — it should feel heavy for its size, which indicates juiciness.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe apple has a pleasant, mildly sweet fragrance near the stem end.

funFact: There are over 7,500 varieties of apples grown worldwide, but only about 100 are commercially grown in the United States.
storageTip: Store in the fridge crisper drawer for up to 6 weeks. Keep them away from other produce, as apples release ethylene gas that speeds ripening.

name: Strawberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly bright red from top to bottom. Avoid berries with white or green tips — they won’t ripen further after picking.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Ripe strawberries have an unmistakable sweet, fragrant aroma. No scent usually means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Leaves
ripenessTips.description: The green cap should be fresh and bright, not wilted or dried out. Berries with intact caps last longer.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard, with a slight give. Mushy berries are overripe and will spoil quickly.

funFact: Strawberries are the only fruit with seeds on the outside, averaging about 200 seeds per berry.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a single layer in the fridge for 3–5 days. Wash only right before eating to prevent mold.

name: Blueberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep blue-purple with a dusty, silvery-white bloom on the surface. That bloom is natural and a sign of freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firm, springing back slightly when gently squeezed. Soft, wrinkled berries are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Container
ripenessTips.description: Shake the container gently — ripe berries should move freely. If they clump together, they may be crushed or moldy underneath.

funFact: Blueberries are one of the only natural foods that are truly blue in color, thanks to the pigment anthocyanin.
storageTip: Store unwashed in their original container in the fridge for up to 10 days. Rinse just before eating.

name: Peach

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe peach has a strong, sweet, floral fragrance at the stem end. If it doesn’t smell like anything, it won’t taste like much either.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should yield slightly to gentle pressure, like a tennis ball. If rock-hard, leave it on the counter to ripen for a day or two.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Look for a creamy or golden background color, not green. The red blush doesn’t indicate ripeness — it’s just where the sun hit.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: The area around the stem should be slightly soft and fragrant. A hard, green stem area means it needs more time.

funFact: Peaches are a member of the rose family, which is why their blossoms look and smell so similar to wild roses.
storageTip: Ripen on the counter at room temperature stem-side down. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Watermelon

ripenessTips.title: Tap It
ripenessTips.description: Knock on the watermelon — a ripe one produces a deep, hollow sound. An unripe melon sounds more metallic and high-pitched.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Field Spot
ripenessTips.description: Flip it over and look at the spot where it rested on the ground. A creamy yellow spot means it ripened in the sun; a white spot means it was picked too early.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe watermelon should feel surprisingly heavy for its size — it’s 92% water when fully ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The rind should be firm and resist scratching with a fingernail. A dull (not shiny) surface often indicates ripeness.

funFact: Watermelon is both a fruit and a vegetable — it’s related to cucumbers, pumpkins, and squash.
storageTip: Store whole at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. Once cut, wrap tightly and refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Mango

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff near the stem end — a ripe mango has a sweet, fruity, almost floral aroma. No scent means it’s not ready yet.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gently squeeze — it should give slightly, like a ripe avocado. Rock-hard mangoes need several days on the counter.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color varies by variety, so don’t rely on red blush. Look for plump, rounded shape and smooth, taut skin without wrinkles.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe mango feels heavy for its size, which indicates high juice and sugar content.

funFact: Mangoes are the most consumed fruit in the world, with over 400 varieties grown across tropical regions.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until fragrant and slightly soft. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Orange

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Pick it up — a ripe orange is heavy for its size, which means it’s full of juice. Compare a few to find the heaviest.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but yield very slightly to pressure. The skin should feel smooth and thin rather than thick and puffy.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe orange has a bright citrus scent even through the peel. Stronger fragrance means more flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin color doesn’t always indicate ripeness — some ripe oranges have green patches. Focus on firmness and weight instead.

funFact: The color orange was actually named after the fruit, not the other way around — before that, English speakers called it “geoluhread” (yellow-red).
storageTip: Store at room temperature for about a week, or refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. They juice best at room temperature.

name: Cherry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep, glossy, and dark — the darker the cherry, the sweeter the flavor. Avoid dull, shriveled, or leaking fruit.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and plump, not soft or mushy. Gently squeeze one — it should resist slightly.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: Fresh cherries have green, flexible stems firmly attached. Brown or brittle stems mean they’ve been sitting too long.

funFact: It takes about 250 cherries to make a single cherry pie, and a mature cherry tree can produce enough for 28 pies in one season.
storageTip: Store unwashed with stems attached in the fridge for up to a week. Cherries don’t ripen after picking, so eat them at peak freshness.

name: Grape

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firmly attached to green, flexible stems. A dusty white bloom on the skin is a good sign of freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and snap when you bite in. Wrinkled or soft grapes are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be green and pliable, not brown and brittle. Give the bunch a gentle shake — a few falling off is fine, but many means they’re old.

funFact: A single grapevine can produce enough fruit to make about 10 bottles of wine per year, and some vines live for over 100 years.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a ventilated bag in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. Wash just before eating for the best texture.

name: Pear

ripenessTips.title: Check the Neck
ripenessTips.description: Press gently near the stem (the neck). If it yields slightly, it’s ripe. Pears ripen from the inside out, so the neck ripens first.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color change varies by variety — Bartletts turn yellow, but Bosc and Anjou stay their original color. Don’t rely on color alone.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe pear has a subtle, sweet fragrance near the stem. Strong perfume means it’s very ripe and should be eaten immediately.

funFact: Pears are one of the few fruits that ripen better off the tree — if left on the branch, they develop gritty stone cells and mealy texture.
storageTip: Buy firm and ripen at room temperature for 2–5 days. Once the neck yields to gentle pressure, refrigerate and eat within 3 days.

name: Banana

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Bright yellow with a few small brown speckles means peak sweetness. Green tips mean it needs another day or two to ripen.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard. The peel should come away easily without tearing the flesh when you open it.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: Look at where individual bananas connect to the bunch. A bright yellow stem with no dark spots means freshly ripe.

funFact: Bananas are technically berries, while strawberries are not — botanically, a berry must come from a single ovary flower.
storageTip: Keep at room temperature until ripe. To slow ripening, separate them and wrap each stem in plastic wrap. Refrigerate ripe bananas — the peel darkens but the fruit stays good for several days.

name: Pineapple

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the base — a ripe pineapple has a strong, sweet, tropical aroma. No scent means it was picked too early; a fermented smell means it’s overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The shell should be golden-yellow from the base upward. More yellow means more ripe. Avoid ones that are entirely green or have dark, soft spots.

ripenessTips.title: Pull a Leaf
ripenessTips.description: Tug gently on a center leaf from the crown. If it slides out easily, the pineapple is ripe. If it holds tight, it needs more time.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, indicating it’s juicy and ripe inside.

funFact: A pineapple is not a single fruit but a cluster of up to 200 individual fruitlets fused together around a central core.
storageTip: Store whole at room temperature for 1–2 days. Once cut, refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Pineapples do not ripen further after harvest.

name: Avocado

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Cradle it in your palm and squeeze gently. A ripe avocado yields to firm, gentle pressure but doesn’t feel mushy. Press with your whole hand to avoid bruising.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Hass avocados darken from green to nearly black when ripe. Other varieties stay green, so rely on feel instead of color for those.

ripenessTips.title: Check Under the Stem
ripenessTips.description: Flick off the small stem cap. If it pops off easily and you see bright green underneath, it’s ripe. Brown underneath means it’s overripe.

funFact: Avocados never ripen on the tree — farmers can leave them hanging for months as a form of natural storage until they’re ready to harvest.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature for 3–5 days. To speed it up, place in a paper bag with a banana. Refrigerate ripe avocados for up to 3 days.

name: Tomato

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly deep red (or the target color for the variety) with smooth, taut skin. Avoid cracks, blemishes, or green shoulders.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should yield slightly to gentle pressure but spring back. Too firm means underripe; too soft means mealy and overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the stem end — a great tomato smells earthy, sweet, and distinctly “tomato-y.” No aroma usually means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe tomato feels heavy for its size, which indicates lots of juice and developed sugars inside.

funFact: Tomatoes were once believed to be poisonous in Europe because wealthy people got sick eating them off lead-containing pewter plates.
storageTip: Never refrigerate unripe tomatoes — cold kills their flavor and texture. Store stem-side down on the counter. Refrigerate only once fully ripe, and bring to room temperature before eating.

name: Corn

ripenessTips.title: Feel the Kernels
ripenessTips.description: Through the husk, feel for plump, firm, evenly spaced kernels all the way to the tip. Gaps or flat spots mean poor pollination.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Silk
ripenessTips.description: The silk (tassels) should be brown and slightly sticky, not dried out or black. Fresh silk means the corn was recently picked.

ripenessTips.title: Look at the Husk
ripenessTips.description: The husk should be bright green, tightly wrapped, and slightly damp. Dry, yellowed husks mean the corn is old.

funFact: Corn always has an even number of rows on each ear, typically between 8 and 22 rows.
storageTip: Eat as soon as possible — corn’s sugar starts converting to starch within hours of picking. Store unhusked in the fridge for up to 3 days.

name: Zucchini

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Choose small to medium zucchini (6–8 inches). The skin should be dark green, glossy, and free of nicks or soft spots. Bigger is not better — large ones are watery and seedy.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm along the entire length with no soft or spongy areas. The skin should resist a light scratch with your fingernail.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: A small stub of stem should still be attached. A freshly cut stem end means it was recently harvested.

funFact: A single zucchini plant can produce 6 to 10 pounds of fruit over a growing season, which is why gardeners are famously eager to give them away.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a perforated bag in the fridge crisper drawer for up to a week. Don’t seal it airtight — zucchini needs airflow to prevent mold.

name: Broccoli

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The floret clusters should be tight, compact, and dark green to deep blue-green. Yellow or open florets mean it’s past its prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The stalks should be firm and rigid, snapping cleanly if bent. Limp, rubbery stalks mean the broccoli is old.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should have a fresh, mild vegetal scent. A strong, sulfurous, or sour smell means it’s starting to go bad.

funFact: Broccoli is a human invention — it was bred by Italian farmers from wild cabbage over 2,000 years ago through selective cultivation.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the fridge crisper drawer for up to 5 days. Don’t wash before storing — moisture promotes mold.

name: Carrot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be a deep, vivid orange with smooth skin. Avoid carrots with cracks, splits, or green shoulders (which taste bitter).

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be rock-firm and rigid — a fresh carrot snaps cleanly when bent. Bendy, rubbery carrots have lost their moisture.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Greens
ripenessTips.description: If the tops are still attached, they should be bright green and perky, not wilted or slimy. Remove greens before storing — they sap moisture from the root.

funFact: Carrots were originally purple or white — the familiar orange variety was developed by Dutch growers in the 17th century.
storageTip: Remove any green tops, then store in a sealed bag in the fridge crisper drawer for up to 3 weeks. Wrap in a damp paper towel to maintain crispness.

name: Spinach

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be vibrant dark green, crisp, and springy. Avoid yellowed, wilted, or slimy leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be crisp and resilient to the touch, not limp or soggy. Fresh spinach holds its shape when lifted.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should smell fresh and earthy with no sour or musty odor. Off smells mean it’s starting to decay.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stems
ripenessTips.description: Stems should be thin and flexible, not thick or woody. Thick stems can indicate the plant bolted and the leaves may be bitter.

funFact: Spinach loses about 90% of its vitamin C within 24 hours of being picked, which is why locally grown spinach is so much more nutritious.
storageTip: Store loosely in a dry paper towel inside an open bag in the fridge. Use within 5–7 days. Don’t wash until ready to use.

name: Bell Pepper

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have vibrant, saturated color (red, yellow, or orange are riper and sweeter than green) with glossy, wrinkle-free skin.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy and firm with thick, rigid walls. Soft spots or wrinkled skin mean it’s losing moisture and freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A good pepper feels surprisingly heavy for its size, which means thick, juicy walls with plenty of flesh.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be green, fresh, and firmly attached. A brown, dried-out stem is a sign of age.

funFact: Green bell peppers are just unripe red peppers — as they mature on the vine, they turn yellow, then orange, then red, getting sweeter at each stage.
storageTip: Store whole in the fridge crisper drawer for up to 2 weeks. Once cut, wrap tightly in plastic and use within 3–4 days.

name: Eggplant

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be smooth, glossy, and deep purple (for common varieties) without wrinkles, scars, or dull patches.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently with your thumb — the flesh should spring back immediately. If the dent stays, it’s overripe. It should feel firm but not rock-hard.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, which indicates fresh, dense flesh rather than dried-out, spongy interior.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Cap
ripenessTips.description: The green calyx (cap) at the top should be bright green and fresh-looking, not brown or dried out.

funFact: Eggplant gets its English name from early European varieties that were small, white, and egg-shaped, looking like eggs hanging from the plant.
storageTip: Store at room temperature if using within 2 days. For longer storage, place in the fridge crisper drawer for up to a week, but use quickly — cold damages the texture over time.

name: Sweet Potato

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Choose smooth-skinned sweet potatoes with even color and no cracks, bruises, or soft spots. Tapered ends are normal.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm all over with no give or soft areas. Soft spots lead to rapid spoilage and often indicate internal rot.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Choose medium-sized ones that feel dense and heavy. Very large sweet potatoes can be fibrous and starchy inside.

funFact: Sweet potatoes are not related to regular potatoes at all — they belong to the morning glory family, while potatoes are nightshades.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place (not the fridge) for up to a month. Cold temperatures cause the starches to convert and create an unpleasant, hard center.

name: Asparagus

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Tips should be tight, compact, and deep green or purple. Avoid spears with open, feathery, or mushy tips — they’re past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Stalks should be firm, straight, and rigid, snapping cleanly when bent. Limp, bendy spears are old and will be tough and fibrous.

ripenessTips.title: Check the Cut Ends
ripenessTips.description: The cut ends should look fresh and moist, not dried out, cracked, or woody. Fresher cuts mean more recently harvested.

funFact: An asparagus spear can grow up to 10 inches in a single 24-hour period under ideal spring conditions.
storageTip: Trim the ends and stand the bunch upright in a jar with an inch of water, then cover loosely with a plastic bag. Refrigerate for up to a week.

name: Fig

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: A ripe fig is soft and yields to gentle pressure, like a water balloon. Firm figs are underripe and won’t have much flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump with rich color (deep purple, brown, or green depending on variety). A slight droop at the neck and small cracks near the bottom are signs of peak ripeness.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should smell mildly sweet and honey-like. A sour or fermented smell means it’s gone too far.

funFact: Figs are technically inverted flowers — the flower blooms inside the fleshy structure, and each tiny seed-like crunch is an individual fruit.
storageTip: Eat immediately or within 1–2 days — figs are extremely perishable. Store in a single layer on a paper towel-lined plate in the fridge.

name: Pomegranate

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe pomegranate feels remarkably heavy for its size — that weight comes from hundreds of juice-filled arils packed inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The skin should be deep red and slightly rough or leathery, not smooth. A slightly angular shape (not perfectly round) means the arils are plump and pressing outward.

ripenessTips.title: Tap It
ripenessTips.description: Tap the side — a ripe pomegranate produces a metallic, hollow sound, indicating the arils inside are juicy and well-developed.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The skin should be firm and taut but not rock-hard. A slight give is fine, but soft spots mean it’s overripe inside.

funFact: A single pomegranate contains about 600 to 800 individual arils (seeds), and the name literally means “apple of many seeds” in Latin.
storageTip: Store whole at room temperature for up to a week, or refrigerate for up to 2 months. Separated arils keep in an airtight container in the fridge for about 5 days.
